```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# Data ---------------------------------
frogs <- read.csv("../../data/ReedfrogSizepred.csv")

# Act 1's grid-search-optimized Ricker ---------------------------------
a_rk <- 1; b_rk <- 0.15
ricker <- function(x, a, b) a * x * exp(-b * x)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines) for equation manipulation /
# show-your-work; pair with fig.height set to however much room is needed
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}

# draws a table with given headers/body for handwritten answers ("" = blank
# cell); headers/values may be plotmath expressions for math; pair with
# fig.height = header_height + nrow(body) * row_height
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                         header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                         cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0)) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    fnt <- if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, font = fnt, cex = cex)
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}
```

```{r key-helpers, include=FALSE}
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
# redraws blank_table() so cells flagged TRUE in `ans` use the answer color
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0), ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && isTRUE(ans[[i]][[j]])
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    font = if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}
```

```{r key-values, include=FALSE}
f2 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 2)
flex_ricker <- function(x, a, p, c) a * x^c * exp(-c * x / p)
holling4 <- function(x, a, b, c) a * x^2 / (b + c * x + x^2)
mn <- aggregate(Kill ~ TBL, data = frogs, FUN = mean)
ssr <- function(pred) sum((mn$Kill - pred)^2)
ssr_vals <- c(ssr(ricker(mn$TBL, 1, 0.15)),
              ssr(flex_ricker(mn$TBL, 3.68e-19, 12.52, 28.72)),
              ssr(holling4(mn$TBL, 0.0329, 115.09, -21.49)))
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta.}


## Picking up where we left off

In Act 1 you built a grid search and found the parameters that minimize SSR for the 2-parameter Ricker function: $a=1$, $b=0.15$, SSR $=6.74$ -- better than any single hand guess (note: your SSR might differ if you used individual residuals instead of the aggregated residuals, but the overall result should be the same). But look closely at the curve below: it never really rises to meet the peak at 12 mm. With only five aggregated data points, three of them at or near zero, and just two parameters that jointly control the curve's peak location, height, and decay rate all at once, the Ricker family doesn't have enough flexibility to chase the one high point without doing worse everywhere else -- so the best fit solution works hard to fit the low points instead of tracking the peak. That's a limitation of the Ricker *shape*. And maybe that's a good reason to ask whether Ricker is even the right family to begin with!

```{r recap-curve, fig.height=3.2, fig.width=5.5}
set.seed(1)
x_j <- frogs$TBL + runif(nrow(frogs), -0.6, 0.6)
plot(x_j, frogs$Kill, xlim = c(5, 40), ylim = c(-0.3, 5.3),
     xlab = "Tadpole size, TBL (mm)", ylab = "Number killed (out of 10)",
     pch = 21, bg = "grey70", cex = 1.4)
curve(ricker(x, a_rk, b_rk), from = 5, to = 40, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue", add = TRUE)
grid()
legend("topright", legend = "Act 1 best-fit Ricker (SSR = 6.74)", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

But finding the best Ricker doesn't tell us whether Ricker is even the right *family* of function to begin with. Today we'll meet two more candidates from the 'bestiary' and compare them against Ricker's best possible fit -- not against a guess.

**Before you do anything else: close your laptop and put away your phone.** Part 1 and the group check-in that follows are pen-and-paper only -- no exceptions. You'll get clear instructions later in this handout for when it's time to open your laptop and use R.

## Part 1: Two new candidates (individual, ~15 min)

**Candidate 1: a flexible Ricker.** Generalize the Ricker function by adding a shape exponent $c$, and reparameterize so the peak location $p$ is a parameter you can set directly (just like you might want to specify "the peak is at 12 mm" instead of "b = 0.15"):

$$y = a\,x^{c}\,e^{-cx/p}$$

**1a.** Check that this really is a generalization-- that is, that the standard Ricker can be 'recovered' from this function. If you set $c=1$, what does this formula reduce to, and how does $p$ relate to Ricker's parameter $b$?

\ans{With $c = 1$: $y = a\,x\,e^{-x/p}$, the plain Ricker with $b = 1/p$ (so $p = 1/b$).}

**1b.** Find $dy/dx$ for the flexible Ricker (product rule together with the chain rule for the exponential term -- same tools as Lab 1's Ricker derivative), and show that the critical point occurs at $x=p$, confirming $p$ really is the peak location.

*Reminders:* $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,e^{g(x)} = g'(x)\,e^{g(x)}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,x^c = c\,x^{c-1}$

Show your work:

\ansbegin

With $u = x^c$, $v = e^{-cx/p}$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = a\left[c\,x^{c-1}e^{-cx/p} + x^c e^{-cx/p}\left(-\frac{c}{p}\right)\right] = a\,c\,x^{c-1}e^{-cx/p}\left(1 - \frac{x}{p}\right)$$
For $x > 0$, only the last factor can be zero: $1 - x/p = 0$, so $x = p$.

\ansend

**Candidate 2: Holling type IV.** This one comes from the *rational-function* branch of the bestiary rather than the exponential branch -- originally used for predator functional responses, but we're borrowing it here purely for its shape:

$$y = \frac{a\,x^2}{b + cx + x^2}, \qquad c < 0$$

Its peak occurs at $x^* = -2b/c$.

*A heads-up if you go looking this up on your own:* some other sources define "Holling type IV" with a plain $x$ in the numerator instead of $x^2$. That version behaves differently at large $x$ -- it declines all the way to zero instead of leveling off at $a$. We're using Bolker's version here, matching your assigned reading.

**1c.** For $b=115.09$, $c=-21.49$, compute the peak location $x^*$:

$x^* =$ \ans{$-2(115.09)/(-21.49) \approx `r round(-2 * 115.09 / -21.49, 2)`$ mm}

Now use the same "throw out the lower-order terms" trick from Monday's lecture to figure out what this function does as $x\to\infty$ (hint: compare the highest powers of $x$ in the numerator and denominator). Is the answer the same as what happens to the Ricker family as $x\to\infty$?

\ans{$y \to ax^2/x^2 = a$: it levels off at $a$ (a positive floor). Not the same: the Ricker family declines to 0.}

**1d. Write the R functions.** Define both candidates as R functions below, following the same pattern as the `ricker` function (`x` first, then parameters). You're writing this by hand on paper, so it doesn't need to run yet -- just get the structure and syntax right.

```
flex_ricker <- function(x, a, p, c){
  
  
}

holling4 <- function(x, a, b, c){


}
```

\ansbegin

```
flex_ricker <- function(x, a, p, c){
  a * x^c * exp(-c * x / p)
}

holling4 <- function(x, a, b, c){
  a * x^2 / (b + c * x + x^2)
}
```

\ansend

## Part 2: Implement and compare (laptops, ~15-20 min)

**2a.** Type up `flex_ricker` and `holling4` in an R script based on what your group wrote in 1d. Here are the actual fitted (SSR-minimizing) parameter values for each family, found the same way you found Act 1's Ricker optimum: $a=3.68\times10^{-19}$, $p=12.52$, $c=28.72$ for the flexible Ricker, and $a=0.0329$, $b=115.09$, $c=-21.49$ for Holling type IV. Plot all three candidates (Act 1's best-fit Ricker, flexible Ricker, Holling IV) overlaid on the tadpole data with `curve(..., add = TRUE)`. If one of these looks a little wild once it's plotted, that's not a bug in your code!

```{r ans-three-curves, fig.height=3.4, fig.width=5.5}
set.seed(1)
x_j <- frogs$TBL + runif(nrow(frogs), -0.6, 0.6)
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(x_j, frogs$Kill, xlim = c(5, 40), ylim = c(-0.3, 5.3),
     xlab = "Tadpole size, TBL (mm)", ylab = "Number killed (out of 10)",
     pch = 21, bg = "grey70", cex = 1.4)
curve(ricker(x, 1, 0.15), from = 5, to = 40, lwd = 2, col = ans_col, add = TRUE)
curve(flex_ricker(x, 3.68e-19, 12.52, 28.72), from = 5, to = 40, lwd = 2, lty = 2,
      col = ans_col, add = TRUE, n = 500)
curve(holling4(x, 0.0329, 115.09, -21.49), from = 5, to = 40, lwd = 2, lty = 3,
      col = ans_col, add = TRUE, n = 500)
legend("topright", c("Ricker", "Flexible Ricker", "Holling IV"), lty = 1:3, lwd = 2,
       col = ans_col, bty = "n")
```

**2b.** Compute the sum of squared residuals (SSR) for all three candidates at the five tank sizes (9, 12, 21, 25, 37 mm) -- your laptop's already open, so use R, a calculator app, Excel, whatever's fastest, rather than doing it by hand like Lab 1 Act 3. Record your results:

```{r fill-ssr-table, fig.height=0.35+3*0.5, fig.width=5.5}
blank_table(
  headers = list("Candidate", "SSR"),
  body = list(
    list("Ricker (a=1, b=0.15, Act 1's best fit)", f2(ssr_vals[1])),
    list("Flexible Ricker", f2(ssr_vals[2])),
    list("Holling type IV", f2(ssr_vals[3]))
  ),
  col_widths = c(2.6, 1),
  cex = 0.9,
  ans = rep(list(c(FALSE, TRUE)), 3)
)
```

**2c.** Which candidate looks best by eye, and which has the lowest SSR? Did this match your group's prediction?

\ans{By eye: the flexible Ricker (a smooth hump). Lowest SSR: Holling IV (`r f2(ssr_vals[3])`), whose curve is a narrow, implausible spike. "Looks best" and "lowest SSR" point to different candidates.}

**2d.** All three curves above are truly optimized this time. Nobody guessed any of these parameter values; each is the true SSR-minimizing fit for its family. And yet the lowest-SSR curve is probably not the one you'd point to as the best *model*. What's going on? (Hint: think about how many data points you have -- five, aggregated tank means -- versus how many free parameters each family gets to work with.) Does the lowest SSR always mean the best model? What would you want to check before trusting a model that fits its own training data almost perfectly?

\ans{With 5 data points and 3 free parameters, a flexible family can nearly pass through every point whether or not its shape makes biological sense (overfitting). Lowest SSR is not always the best model. Check how it predicts data it wasn't fit to, and how stable its parameters are when the data are resampled.}

For Act 3, we're going back to the plain Ricker -- not because it won this comparison outright, but because a 2-parameter model is easier to reason about (and to bootstrap) than one flexible enough to bend itself into whatever shape the data demands. We'll ask a different question: how much should we actually trust the specific $(a,b)$ Act 1 found?
